title: Stalling the production line:  How late arrivals hold up production, and why firms tolerate it. Guest post by Shreya Chandra
gist: Job-market paper (Shreya Chandra, UC Berkeley) RCT in 92 small Tiruppur garment firms: paying a 20%-of-earnings punctuality bonus raised on-time arrival 21 p.p. and worker output 24% (firm output 29%, orders 21%, delivery delays -40%) via production-line coordination spillovers, yet cut profits 5% net of incentives; worker demand for flexibility stems from poor public services and missing care markets, implying infrastructure as industrial policy.

insights.claim: Small garment factories in Tiruppur, South India, typically employ 6 workers, 85% of whom live within a 15-minute commute, and run batch processing lines where each worker performs one operation and passes bundles onward.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Line production makes small-firm output hostage to the slowest/latest worker.

insights.claim: Workers in these Tiruppur factories arrive late on 43% of worker-days, with arrival times ranging from 3 hours before to 3 hours after start time.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Lateness is a pervasive, measurable productivity drag in EM informal manufacturing.
insights.quote: workers arrive late at work on 43% of worker-days

insights.claim: Late arrivals reflect preference for flexibility among a workforce averaging 37 years old, 45% female, 94% married and 84% with a child under 14.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Labor supply constraints from care duties shape firm organization in EM manufacturing.

insights.claim: Most firms pay operation-specific piece rates with no incentive tied to finished garments, and neither reward punctuality nor penalize lateness.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Contract design does not internalize coordination externalities.

themes.theme: RCT results: punctuality spills over to the whole line

insights.claim: In an experiment across 92 firms and 600 workers, a daily incentive worth 20% of average daily earnings for arriving on time raised on-time arrival by 21 percentage points against a control mean of 58%, driven entirely by previously late workers.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Moderate-size incentives move behavior substantially among the marginal late workers.
insights.locator: Workers in treatment firms are nearly 40%

insights.claim: Workers in treated firms produced 24% more output per week (about 930 extra pieces), and output rose similarly even for early workers who did not change arrival times, indicating within-firm spillovers.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Coordination failures, not individual effort, can be the binding productivity constraint.
insights.quote: workers in treatment firms produce 24% more output per week
insights.locator: As a result, workers in treatment firms

insights.claim: In 'Bottleneck' firms where a late worker performed upstream tasks, worker output rose 32% versus 12% in non-bottleneck firms, and early workers gained about 33% only in bottleneck firms, showing the spillover comes from better line coordination.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Upstream bottlenecks are where punctuality interventions pay off most.
insights.quote: spillovers to “early” workers are only present in Bottleneck firms
insights.locator: Effects on worker output are larger

insights.claim: Treated firms produced 29% more total output, procured 21% more new orders and cut delivery delays by 40%.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Reliability gains translate into demand, relevant to supplier selection in apparel supply chains.
insights.quote: Treatment firms produce 29% more in total output, procure 21% more new orders, and reduce delivery delays by 40%.

insights.claim: Excluding incentive payments weekly profits would rise 8%, but paying the 20% incentive reduced weekly profits by 5%, and about a quarter of treated workers still arrived late.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Punctuality is valuable but too expensive to buy with cash bonuses alone.
insights.quote: paying the 20% incentives I offered reduces weekly profits by 5%

insights.claim: Treated firm owners acknowledged the benefits but were only willing to pay incentives worth 5% of daily earnings, and a year later did little beyond verbal encouragement.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Intervention effects fade without durable contract changes.

insights.claim: The labor market is segmented: large firms enforce strict schedules and hire younger migrant workers, while small firms compete for experienced local workers by offering flexibility; 52% of owners believe strict rules without extra pay would raise attrition.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Flexibility functions as a non-wage compensation that small firms cannot unilaterally withdraw.
insights.quote: half of firm owners (52%) believe that strict rules without extra pay would increase worker attrition
insights.locator: Why can’t firms enforce timely arrival

themes.theme: Infrastructure and care markets as industrial policy

insights.claim: Workers cite missing markets for household and care services and daily volatility from unreliable public services (electricity, water, lack of school buses) as reasons they need flexible schedules, with women and carers showing stronger preference.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Public infrastructure quality feeds directly into manufacturing productivity.

insights.claim: Improving public services, infrastructure and childcare could reduce lateness and accelerate small-firm growth, making such policies effective industrial policy.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Care-economy and utility investment can be a lever for EM manufacturing scale-up.
insights.quote: Policies aimed at improving public services and infrastructure could reduce worker lateness and consequently accelerate firm growth.
